lead: A software product does not appear in one jump. It moves through a life cycle: a set of phases, each with a purpose, a main output and a check before the next phase. This life cycle exists because a large product cannot be understood, built and trusted in one pass. It is used on every project, from a college fee portal to a railway reservation system, to plan effort, assign people and decide when work is good enough to move forward.
prereq: You need: 1.1 and 1.2; this chapter assumes software is programs, data and documents, and that engineering practice is layered.

sections.h3: What the life cycle is and how it starts

blocks.text: Software development life cycle (SDLC) is the set of phases a software product passes through, from the decision to build it to retirement. A phase is a group of related work with one main output and a check called an exit criterion. The check stops a weak output from moving forward.

Initiation decides whether the project should exist. Its output is a project charter: a short authorisation that names the sponsor, the goal, the rough budget and the scope boundary. People involved are the sponsor, product owner, project manager and a technical lead. Exit criterion: the charter is signed and the scope is agreed. A feasibility study starts here and continues into requirements: is the idea technically possible, is the benefit worth the cost, is it legal, and can it finish in time? Unit 2 covers requirements and feasibility in depth; Unit 6 covers charter and scheduling.

Requirements states what the system must do and how well it must do it. Output: software requirements specification (SRS). People: business analyst, users, test lead. Exit criterion: the SRS is reviewed and baselined, so later changes are controlled.

sections.h3: Design and construction: deciding how, then building

blocks.text: Design converts requirements into a plan for the software. It fixes the architecture (layers, services, data stores), the modules, their interfaces and the main data structures. Output: a design description, often with UML diagrams. People: architects, designers, database administrator. Exit criterion: a design review confirms that every requirement is covered and that quality attributes such as security and response time have a planned solution. Unit 3 teaches design and UML.

Construction writes the code and the unit tests for each module. Output: source code, a build and unit test results. People: programmers, a build engineer and testers who review unit tests. Exit criterion: the code compiles, unit tests pass and a code review is closed. Construction is not always the largest phase; a project that reuses a large platform may spend more effort on requirements and integration.
Design and construction can overlap. A team may design module A, start coding it, and design module B in parallel. Overlap is safe only when the interface between A and B is fixed early.

Testing checks the assembled product at increasing scope: unit test checks one module, integration test checks modules together, system test checks the whole product against the SRS, and acceptance test checks that the customer will accept it. Output: test results, a defect log and a release recommendation. People: test engineers and, for acceptance, real users. Exit criterion: planned tests are run and defect levels meet the agreed threshold. Unit 4 covers the techniques.

Deployment moves the tested product into the user environment. Output: a release package, installation or migration steps and user training. People: release engineer, operations and support desk. Exit criterion: users can log in, complete a core task, and the support desk has the release notes.

Maintenance keeps the product useful after go-live. It covers corrective fixes, adaptive changes (a new tax rule or phone model), perfective improvements and preventive work. Output: patches and later releases. People: maintenance programmers and support staff. Exit criterion: the change is verified and the release is recorded.

Phases overlap and repeat. A change after go-live does not stop at code: it goes back to requirements, then design, construction and testing. The waterfall model draws phases as a strict sequence; incremental and spiral models repeat groups of phases. See 1.5.

examples.question: A college fee portal is estimated at 200 person-days. The plan splits effort as requirements 15%, design 20%, construction 40%, testing 20% and deployment 5%. (a) Compute person-days per phase. (b) After go-live, a new fee rule is needed. Which phase does the work return to first, and why?
steps: Check: 30 + 40 + 80 + 40 + 10 = 200 person-days, so the split uses the full estimate.

A new fee rule changes what the system must do, so the work returns to requirements first. It then passes through design, construction, testing and deployment as needed. Maintenance is not only a code edit.
examples.answer: 30, 40, 80, 40 and 10 person-days; they sum to 200 person-days. The new fee rule sends work back to requirements first.

traps: Assuming testing starts only after all coding ends. Unit, integration and system testing often overlap construction and design.
Treating phases as strictly sequential and never repeated. A requirement change after go-live sends work back to requirements, then design, construction and testing.
Confusing maintenance with bug fixing only. Maintenance also covers adaptive, perfective and preventive changes.
Mixing up phase outputs: requirements produces the SRS, design produces the design description, and construction produces code and unit test results.
Believing construction always takes the largest share of effort. Reuse-heavy or compliance-heavy projects can spend more on requirements, integration or testing.

quiz.q: List the seven life cycle phases in the order used in this chapter.
quiz.a: Initiation, requirements, design, construction, testing, deployment, maintenance.

quiz.q: Why does each phase need an exit criterion?
quiz.a: An exit criterion is a check that the phase output is complete and good enough. It prevents incomplete or weak work from entering the next phase, where it becomes costlier to fix.

quiz.q: A project of 500 person-days is split as requirements 10%, design 20%, construction 45%, testing 20% and deployment 5%. Compute person-days per phase and the sum.
A bank adds a new UPI payment rule six months after release. Explain which phases are repeated and why maintenance alone is not enough.
quiz.a: The rule is a new requirement, so requirements is repeated to define it. Design must change the payment module and interfaces, construction writes the code, testing checks the new rule and regression, and deployment releases it. Maintenance is the trigger and support context, but the work itself repeats the earlier phases.

quiz.q: Which phase produces the SRS, and which phase produces the design description?
quiz.a: Requirements produces the SRS. Design produces the design description, often with UML diagrams.

quiz.q: Why can design and construction overlap safely only when module interfaces are fixed early?
quiz.a: Two modules built in parallel must agree on the calls, data formats and error behaviour. If the interface changes later, both modules need rework. Fixing the interface first lets teams design and code different modules at the same time without breaking each other.

quiz.q: Name the four feasibility questions asked during initiation and early requirements.
quiz.a: Technical feasibility, economic feasibility, legal feasibility and schedule feasibility.

quiz.q: What are the four kinds of maintenance work?
quiz.a: Corrective, adaptive, perfective and preventive maintenance.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the SDLC is now usually run with continuous integration and continuous delivery, so deployment becomes a small repeated step rather than one large event. Regulated products, such as medical devices or banking software, add formal traceability from each requirement to design, code and test evidence. Modern curricula also connect the SDLC to DevOps, platform engineering and model-based systems engineering. Search next for "software development life cycle traceability" and "continuous delivery deployment pipeline".
